full_judgment: 8. Mr. Khandker has referred to two decisions in which some statutes or governmental actions have been held to be fraud upon some other statutes. In the Supreme Court Appeals (Ind.) 1952, page 53, the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950, so far as it relates to the provision for compensation for rent receiving stales compulsorily acquired by the Government has been held to be ultra vires and a fraud on the Constitution of India, 1950 which provides that no private property shall be acquired unless compensation is paid recording .to fixed rates or according to principles laying clown. the procedure for fixing such rates. The Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 under which rent receiving estates were compulsorily acquired did provide for payment of compensation but the provisions were found to be vague and indefinite. Mr. P.R. Das, learned counsel for the affected landlords relying on a decision in the South Wales Case, A.C. (1940), 813, contended that the Act pretended to make elaborate provisions for paying compensation but that by shift and contrivance it provided for evasion of its payment. One of the provisions for compensation as made was that the compensation might be paid in 40 installments, without however, mentioning the interval between two installments, leaving it to the description of the state government who, it was argued, might make the interval for 10 years in the circumstances it was held by the Indian Supreme Court that the compensation obligation of paying compensation could be easily voided by the government it was observed:
